{"id": "2:280/q06", "question": "What event prompted this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether an occasion is stated broadly as debt or tied to the particular usury claim.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q06/p1", "position": "After the usury ban, Banu ʿAmr ibn ʿUmayr or Thaqīf demanded principal from Banu al-Mughīra; they sought delay until harvest, were refused, and this verse came.", "reasons": "Muqātil says the Prophet sent the earlier verse to ʿAttāb, who read it to Banu ʿAmr, and they repented. Rāzī identifies four brothers and the threat of war; reports vary in names and detail. Some notes distinguish the request for respite from the rule it occasioned."}, {"id": "2:280/q06/p2", "position": "The verse was revealed concerning usury.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says so in several transmitted routes; the fuller Banu al-Mughīra report explains the usury context."}, {"id": "2:280/q06/p3", "position": "The verse was revealed concerning debt in general.", "reasons": "A report from Ibn ʿAbbās gives debt as its occasion without specifying usury."}]}
{"id": "2:280/q07", "question": "What must a creditor do when the debtor cannot pay?", "turns_on": "Whether hardship is complete inability to pay or strain from realizing assets; when solvency begins.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q07/p1", "position": "Grant time until the debtor can pay; collection then becomes due.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and Qatāda specify principal; Mujāhid and al-Suddī forbid increasing the debt for time, replacing the pre-Islamic increase-or-pay demand. Several sources explain the statement as a binding command. Ibn ʿĀshūr makes obligation certain for complete insolvency; al-Study Quran instead calls the respite encouragement."}, {"id": "2:280/q07/p2", "position": "A usury debtor's principal remains payable once able; a solvent debtor must not delay.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says the legal debt attaches to property; Qurtubī cites 2:279 for a right to principal and seizure of property. Thaʿlabī cites reports that solvent delay is injustice, and Bursevī urges swift repayment even before the deadline."}, {"id": "2:280/q07/p3", "position": "For a debtor in financial strain whose assets could be sold, some require delay and Mālik and the majority recommend it.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes absolute insolvency from hardship caused by an immediate sale that would damage livelihood; later Cordoban judges used discretionary respite to avert harm. The Study Quran speaks of encouragement while retaining principal."}]}
{"id": "2:280/q08", "question": "Which debts receive obligatory respite?", "turns_on": "Whether occasion limits wording, and whether generality is textual or analogical.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q08/p1", "position": "Every insolvent debtor's debt, whether born of usury, sale, loan, or trust, is covered.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī distinguishes the usury occasion from the verse's general ruling, with debt owed from property rather than the body. ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others rely on unrestricted language; Rāzī cites the shared inability to pay; Ibn ʿĀshūr says annulled usury principal has become ordinary debt. Naḥḥās prefers the comprehensive reading."}, {"id": "2:280/q08/p2", "position": "The verse's obligatory respite is specific to a usury debt; ordinary trusts and other debts are to be repaid.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Shurayḥ and Ibrāhīm invoke the usury occasion and 4:58's duty to restore trusts. Shurayḥ even detained a claimant of insolvency; Rāzī's Qāḍī says context and 2:279 favor this reading. Ibn ʿAṭiyya concedes manifest poverty still requires delay. Sources differ on whether al-Ḍaḥḥāk belongs here."}, {"id": "2:280/q08/p3", "position": "The text directly rules on usury debt and the identical rule extends to other debts by analogy.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this reconciliation; Jishumī prefers it because inability to pay is common to both kinds of debt. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the cancelled interest leaves ordinary principal."}]}
{"id": "2:280/q09", "question": "When may an insolvent debtor be imprisoned or pursued?", "turns_on": "Whether insolvency is proven and whether the debt falls under the verse.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q09/p1", "position": "Once insolvency is known, the creditor may neither imprison, press, nor continually restrain the debtor.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says no payable asset is being withheld and a debt cannot be collected from the debtor's person; al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qushayrī exclude prison after insolvency is established. Abū Hurayra and Abū Saʿīd reports are cited; Qurtubī says Abū Qatāda's report bars demand even on credible suspicion without a judge's finding."}, {"id": "2:280/q09/p2", "position": "On a usury-only construction, an ordinary debtor may be held until payment.", "reasons": "Shurayḥ cites 4:58 and argues divine commands cannot conflict; the reported usury-only view permits prison for other claims."}, {"id": "2:280/q09/p3", "position": "A debtor may be detained while a doubtful claim of insolvency is investigated, but released once genuine insolvency is proven.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥanīfa suggests two or three months and private inquiry. Mālik, Shāfiʿī and Ḥanafī jurists allow detention pending proof, while Mālik reserves it for suspected concealment or obstinacy; Rāzī likewise allows detention when status is unclear."}]}
{"id": "2:280/q10", "question": "What qualifies a debtor as insolvent?", "turns_on": "Which assets and necessities count as available means.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q10/p1", "position": "The debtor lacks resources beyond moderate necessities for self and dependents.", "reasons": "Abān and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz still count a person with only a house and no surplus as insolvent. Al-Ṣādiq and Ṭabrisī use economical subsistence; al-Jubbāʾī includes stagnant goods or lack of usable resources. Jishumī includes inability to sell."}, {"id": "2:280/q10/p2", "position": "Any saleable assets must first be used, while only necessary food and clothing are kept.", "reasons": "Rāzī allows sale of a house and spare clothing and requires distressed sale of unsalable goods. Qurtubī gives rules for clothing, disputes over a wife's clothes and a scholar's books, and says homes, servants and Friday clothes can be sold unless of little value; Mālik's transmitted minimum is a covering garment."}, {"id": "2:280/q10/p3", "position": "Jurists disagree whether an able-bodied insolvent person must work or accept another's payment.", "reasons": "Rāzī records both unresolved disputes without preferring either."}]}
{"id": "2:280/q11", "question": "Who must prove or verify insolvency?", "turns_on": "Whether the debtor received property in the transaction, affecting the starting presumption.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q11/p1", "position": "For a sale or loan with value received, the debtor must prove loss or insolvency.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī says receipt creates a presumption of means; Rāzī requires two upright witnesses that the consideration was lost. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān connect the existential construction to treating solvency as the ordinary state."}, {"id": "2:280/q11/p2", "position": "For an obligation without value received, the creditor must prove solvency; an oath or debtor's statement can establish poverty.", "reasons": "Dowry, guarantee and damages supply the examples; the original presumption is poverty. Al-Ḥasan accepts a debtor's sworn claim unless creditors produce evidence or see assets."}]}
{"id": "2:280/q12", "question": "Did this verse end selling an insolvent debtor for debt?", "turns_on": "Whether a valid prior Islamic authorization, rather than merely pre-Islamic custom, can be shown.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q12/p1", "position": "It abrogated an earlier practice of selling or enslaving a debtor unable to pay.", "reasons": "Some scholars identify a pre-Islamic practice; al-Ṭaḥāwī says it also existed early in Islam. {"id": "2:280/q16", "question": "What does 'until ease' mark?", "turns_on": "Whether ease denotes restored resources, death, or payment through public alms.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q16/p1", "position": "Until the debtor gains sufficient wealth or means to repay.", "reasons": "Most commentators derive maysara from yusr, the opposite of hardship. Jishumī connects it to ease of transactions and needs."}, {"id": "2:280/q16/p2", "position": "Until death or separation in a reported use of the term.", "reasons": "Abū Jaʿfar glosses maysara as death in two routes; Ibrāhīm uses it for a marriage term meaning death or separation. {"id": "2:280/q17", "question": "How is maysara formed and read?", "turns_on": "The sīn vowel and whether a rare suffix form is licensed by feminine elision, plural morphology, or a verbal noun.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q17/p1", "position": "Nāfiʿ and, in some reports, Ḥamza and others read ḍamma on sīn.", "reasons": "Authorities differ on the exact reader list: Farisī says Nāfiʿ alone; Bayḍāwī, Biqāʿī and Ālūsī add Ḥamza. Abū ʿAlī accepts the less common pattern and cites masraba/mashriqa; Biqāʿī hears fuller ease in it. Naḥḥās and al-Samīn report grammatical criticism, while Qiraat-ER sees no major shift of meaning."}, {"id": "2:280/q17/p2", "position": "The majority read fatḥa on sīn with final feminine tāʾ and tanwīn in connection.", "reasons": "Sībawayh gives the feminine mafʿala pattern; Ṭabarī compares marḥama and mashʾama. Abū ʿAlī prefers fatḥa as more common; Naḥḥās calls it eloquent Najdī. All readers pronounce tāʾ with tanwīn in connection according to Farisī."}, {"id": "2:280/q17/p3", "position": "A construct or suffix form drops the feminine tāʾ; some read maysarahu or maysūrihi.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, Yaʿqūb and ʿAbd Allāh receive variants. Ibn Jinnī, al-Farrāʾ and al-Samīn explain tāʾ elision before annexation, with poetic ʿidda and Qur'an 24:37 parallels; Abū al-Baqāʾ suggests deleted wāw from maysūra, and al-Akhfash allows a mafʿūl verbal noun. Grammarians dispute singular mafʿal: Sībawayh excludes productive singulars, al-Kisāʾī permits rare cases, and Abū ʿAlī treats maʿūn, maʾlak and makram as plurals. Jamil and ʿAdī provide poetic examples."}, {"id": "2:280/q17/p4", "position": "Maysara is one of several examples where vocalization can change without changing spelling or sense.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba places it among forms distinguished by stem vowels or inflection but not consonantal writing."}]}

{"id": "2:280/q21", "question": "What act is called charity here?", "turns_on": "Whether 'charity' is debt cancellation, the already commanded delay, or a broader gift that includes solvent debtors.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q21/p1", "position": "Forgiving all or part of the insolvent debtor's principal, voluntarily, is better than waiting or collecting.", "reasons": "Ibrāhīm, al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and the majority specify principal; al-Suddī adds al-ʿAbbās's example. Ṭabarī prefers this because the phrase follows the insolvent case; Rāzī and Ālūsī say mere delay is already required, while khayrun commends a new voluntary good. Ibn ʿĀshūr says cancellation relieves distress and restores the debtor's means. Several sources cite 2:237."}, {"id": "2:280/q21/p2", "position": "Giving the debtor further time itself counts as charity and earns a daily charity reward.", "reasons": "The Prophetic report underlies this interpretation in Zamakhsharī, Rāzī, Nasafī, Bayḍāwī and Bursevī. Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī reject it as the meaning of the verse because delay has already been commanded."}, {"id": "2:280/q21/p3", "position": "Charity can cover forgiving principal owed by either rich or poor debtors.", "reasons": "A report ascribed to Qatāda frames it broadly. {"id": "2:280/q22", "question": "Why is remitting debt better for creditors?", "turns_on": "Which benefit the sources foreground: personal reward, social effects, or both.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q22/p1", "position": "It brings praise or blessing now and lasting, greater reward in the next life.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says knowledgeable people recognize its merit; Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān name worldly praise and abundant reward. Bayḍāwī contrasts multiplied lasting reward with money that passes; Biqāʿī adds compensation and blessing. Jishumī says praise here and reward hereafter."}, {"id": "2:280/q22/p2", "position": "It turns the abandoned usurious increase into a real increase through charity.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī ties the verse to 2:276, 30:39 and 3:130: usury takes without compensation, charity gives without it and spreads mercy, maintains the poor, grows wealth, and stabilizes society."}]}
{"id": "2:280/q23", "question": "What does 'if you know' require its audience to know?", "turns_on": "Whether the object of knowledge is the act's value, God's command, or the debtor's condition.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q23/p1", "position": "Knowledge must become action: recognizing divine guidance, then remitting or easing the debt.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī makes it an instruction to recognize and act; Abū Muslim says reasoners grasp God's inducement. Al-Samīn and Ālūsī supply an omitted answer: those who know will act."}, {"id": "2:280/q23/p2", "position": "Know that charity's reward is better than delay, collection, or the money taken.", "reasons": "Jishumī lists divine reward and superiority over delay or collection; Rāzī gives it as a second reading. {"id": "2:280/q25", "question": "What ancillary rulings and warnings accompany debt in these sources?", "turns_on": "The sources extend the verse to adjacent debt ethics and disputed court consequences.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q25/p1", "position": "Borrowers should intend repayment and pay promptly; wrongful delay or borrowing to default is condemned.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī transmits theft for a loan with no intention to repay and injustice for solvent delay. Bursevī says repayment should be hastened, cites guardian angels for intending repayment, and commends borrowing for God’s cause, burial shrouds, or chaste marriage; early Muslims sometimes borrowed while relying on the angel report."}, {"id": "2:280/q25/p2", "position": "A lawful creditor retains a claim, and God remains with the creditor until payment unless the debt funds what God dislikes.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar directed his treasurer to collect after hearing this report. Qushayrī likewise says the established claim persists despite respite."}, {"id": "2:280/q25/p3", "position": "Debt remains morally serious even after major good deeds.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī reports that the Prophet did not pray over a debtor until Abū Qatāda guaranteed seventeen or eighteen dirhams, likened debt to disbelief in gravity, and warned of anxiety, humiliation, divine humbling and severe posthumous sin. Bursevī reports that even martyrdom does not expiate debt, repeated three times."}, {"id": "2:280/q25/p4", "position": "A wife may not obtain separation merely because her husband is poor, according to one legal view.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ, al-Zuhrī and Kufan jurists analogize her claim to a deferred court debt and cite this verse and 24:32."}, {"id": "2:280/q25/p5", "position": "A judge may sell a debtor's assets, but jurists differ on who bears loss before proceeds reach creditors.", "reasons": "Qurtubī says loss after the judge receives proceeds is the creditors' and discharges the debtor; Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam keeps liability on the debtor until creditors receive them. Loss before sale and delivery remains debtor's risk."}, {"id": "2:280/q25/p6", "position": "A loan may itself be superior to alms when it reaches a needy borrower.", "reasons": "Bursevī transmits Umāma's dream of an eighteenfold loan versus tenfold charity; the explanation says charity may reach a rich person whereas a borrower is needy. A separate report promises Paradise entry for lending, pardoning a killer, or repeated recitation of al-Ikhlāṣ."}, {"id": "2:280/q25/p7", "position": "Loans were ideally charitable; credit sales and leases offered investment uses of money over time.", "reasons": "Study Quran distinguishes charitable loans from investment and financing forms."}]}
{"id": "2:280/q26", "question": "How does this command connect to the surrounding usury passage?", "turns_on": "How immediate principal recovery, usury prohibition, and charity frame the conditional.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q26/p1", "position": "After canceling interest while preserving principal, the passage addresses an insolvent debtor and replaces pay-or-increase with delay or remission.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī locates the immediate context among converts owed pre-Islamic usury. Ṭabrisī, Jishumī and Ibn ʿĀshūr explain why the conditional follows principal repayment. Ṭabāṭabāʾī contrasts the pre-Islamic increase on delayed payment. Kuran Yolu distinguishes enforceable principal from moral excellence, and Biqāʿī explains the reciprocal prohibition of wronging."}, {"id": "2:280/q26/p2", "position": "The warning of war against usurers intensifies the surrounding passage; some will persist despite prohibition.", "reasons": "Ḥarallī calls war forceful resistance, and says the Messenger of mercy becomes an adversary to a usurer; Biqāʿī says pairing God and Messenger magnifies the threat and predicts some disobedience."}, {"id": "2:280/q26/p3", "position": "The usury passages are set against neighboring charity material: taking without compensation versus giving without it.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī links 2:276, 2:280, 30:39 and 3:130, arguing opposite social and spiritual consequences."}, {"id": "2:280/q26/p4", "position": "Related usury reports prohibit delayed currency exchange and unequal exchange of like goods.", "reasons": "Al-Durr transmits hand-to-hand currency exchange, the fresh-versus-dried date prohibition because fresh dates shrink, a warning on surplus gold or silver exchange, and Abū Bakra's report of a prohibition two months before the Prophet's death."}]}
{"id": "2:280/q27", "question": "When were the usury verses revealed?", "turns_on": "Which report identifies the last verse or set of verses.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q27/p1", "position": "The usury verse or verses were among the last or the final revelation.", "reasons": "ʿUmar says the Prophet died before explaining them and cautions against doubtful usury; Ibn ʿAbbās calls the usury verse last. {"id": "2:280/q28", "question": "What does Qushayrī draw inwardly from the debt and respite language?", "turns_on": "The movement from an outward debtor to human spiritual need and present accountability.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q28/p1", "position": "Divine mercy grants needy people time, even while God knows their incapacity and sincere dependence on Him.", "reasons": "Qushayrī contrasts an indebted person without assets or business capital with one destitute in livelihood who has only the Master; he also retains the outward creditor's claim and respite."}, {"id": "2:280/q28/p2", "position": "Restraint of desire and reliance on God's promise bring present respite and blessing; returning to blameworthy states brings erasure or punishment.", "reasons": "Qushayrī contrasts deeds undertaken by God's leave with acts driven by caprice and says persistent wrong has no standing with God."}, {"id": "2:280/q28/p3", "position": "The return and reckoning occur at resurrection and inwardly through the heart's accounting with every breath.", "reasons": "Qushayrī says the present demand is more pressing than the promised future reckoning."}]}

{"id": "2:280/q32", "question": "Can Qurʾānic words be foreign in origin?", "turns_on": "Whether earlier foreign origin survives once a term is assimilated into Arabic.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q32/p1", "position": "The Qurʾān contains no foreign vocabulary: its words are Arabic or shared across languages.", "reasons": "Most authorities cite the Qurʾān's description as Arabic; Abū ʿUbayda objects to calling a word Nabataean, Ibn Jarīr explains multilingual glosses as shared terms, and another view invokes Arabic's vastness. {"id": "2:280/q33", "question": "What introductory claims are made about al-Baqara?", "turns_on": "Different introductory descriptions, merits and counts of the sūra.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q33/p1", "position": "It is a Medinan sūra revealed at different times, called the Qurʾān's tent for its stature, beauty, laws and exhortations.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya also reports Ibn ʿUmar's eight years studying its legal sciences, a count of five hundred rulings and fifteen parables, and a claim of 360 meanings of mercy, hope and punishment."}, {"id": "2:280/q33/p2", "position": "Reports call al-Baqara the best or summit sūra, with Āyat al-Kursī its leading verse.", "reasons": "Other reports say Satan avoids a house in which it is recited, it and Āl ʿImrān will defend reciters as clouds or birds, and its last two verses suffice at night. {"id": "2:280/q34", "question": "What does the ancillary word ghamm mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the term stresses covering sorrow or its short duration.", "positions": [{"id": "2:280/q34/p1", "position": "Sorrow that covers the heart, with its root sense of covering.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī relates the root to a covering over neck and forehead and to cloud or a veiled moon; he distinguishes fear before an event, ghamm after it, and recurring worry."}, {"id": "2:280/q34/p2", "position": "A quickly passing distress of the soul.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī transmits this as another definition."}]}
{"id": "3:5/q01", "question": "How is the assertion with inna structured?", "turns_on": "Whether the clauses continue inna's predication or stand independently.", "positions": [{"id": "3:5/q01/p1", "position": "The negative clause is inna's predicate, and repeated predication strengthens the assertion.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī identifies the negative clause as the predicate and notes the emphasis of reiterating the predication."}, {"id": "3:5/q01/p2", "position": "The clauses can be read as independent statements of knowledge, power and will, and exclusive divinity.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān prefers independent clauses but allows them to predicate the preceding inna; he assigns complete knowledge to the first, power and will to the second, and exclusive divinity to the third."}]}

{"id": "3:5/q03", "question": "What does it mean that nothing is hidden from God?", "turns_on": "Whether a particular Christian occasion limits the verse's unrestricted wording.", "positions": [{"id": "3:5/q03/p1", "position": "God knows all things and states, including inward and outward, past, future, possible, particular and universal matters.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Ibn Kathīr include heaven's and earth's inhabitants and their unseen. Al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān and Elmalılı include universals and particulars; Elmalılı adds material and spiritual, inward and outward. {"id": "3:5/q04", "question": "Why say that nothing is hidden rather than simply that God knows?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:5/q04/p1", "position": "The negative form conveys emphatic, exhaustive knowledge in every knowable respect.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says this wording covers every knowable aspect. {"id": "3:5/q05", "question": "How is God's knowledge characterized?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:5/q05/p1", "position": "It is intrinsic, eternal and prior to events, unlike acquired human knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says God knows by His essence, with no knowable respect hidden. {"id": "3:5/q10", "question": "What does in the earth and in the heaven refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the locations name the entire cosmos or serve as figures for outward and inward acts.", "positions": [{"id": "3:5/q10/p1", "position": "Earth and heaven together denote the whole universe and all its locations.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī takes them for the whole domain, and al-Bayḍāwī says they bound human perception. {"id": "3:5/q13", "question": "Why is earth named before heaven?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:5/q13/p1", "position": "The order begins with familiar earthly affairs and ascends to the more remote heaven, focusing the moral warning on people.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī describe an ascent from lower to higher; both stress earthly conduct. {"id": "3:5/q15", "question": "What do the opening verses report about the Najrān delegation?", "turns_on": "Whether the occasion of revelation restricts a general statement.", "positions": [{"id": "3:5/q15/p1", "position": "The opening eighty-odd verses addressed Najrān's Christian delegation after their encounter with the Prophet.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī, Ibn Isḥāq and al-Rabīʿ describe sixty delegates with fourteen notables, including ʿĀqib ʿAbd al-Masīḥ, Sayyid al-Ayham and Bishop Abū Ḥāritha. {"id": "3:5/q16", "question": "Does Jesus' knowledge of hidden things establish divinity?", "turns_on": "Whether knowing some unseen events entails unlimited intrinsic knowledge and independent power.", "positions": [{"id": "3:5/q16/p1", "position": "Christians argued that Jesus' disclosures of unseen private events showed divine knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports their claim and their additional appeal to reviving the dead, healing the blind and leprous, and making a bird from clay by God's permission.
